module_title: Foundation Model Customization, Evaluation and Bedrock Applications
part_title: Evaluating Foundation Models and Business Outcomes
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 09 through 14 individually in order, including example values, numbered stages, metric diagrams and quality/business outcome distinctions.

scenes.title: Automatic foundation-model evaluation
scenes.narration: We now move from adapting a foundation model to measuring whether its answers are good enough. Follow the four numbered stages across the slide. Stage one is to prepare a representative evaluation dataset. Two example tasks are shown: summarize an article, and answer a knowledge question such as 'What is the capital of France?' A reference answer is provided when the chosen scoring metric needs one. Stage two sends these prompts to the selected foundation model through Amazon Bedrock. You can see separate generated answers for summarization and question answering. Stage three is model evaluation, represented by the checklist. An evaluator scores characteristics relevant to the task, such as correctness, relevance or groundedness. Groundedness means that an answer is supported by the available source information rather than inventing facts. Stage four compares scores across models or settings and, importantly, inspects failed examples. Look at the bottom-left comparison of an article summary with a reference summary. Next to it, the question-answering example shows 'The capital of France is Paris' against a reference answer of 'Paris.' The text can differ while the core answer remains correct; this is why a scoring method must fit the task. The bottom considerations note that evaluation is separate from training. Running a model evaluation does not itself update model weights. Support for specific evaluation methods, models and Regions can vary. The main lesson is not to chase one score. Use representative prompts, appropriate metrics and a review of actual mistakes to choose a model that meets your use case.

scenes.title: Build a representative benchmark dataset
scenes.narration: The previous slide introduced an evaluation dataset. This slide shows how to build one you can trust. A benchmark is a fixed, curated set of test cases used to compare models or versions consistently. Start with the first panel on the left. Its five labels are Target users, Tasks, Languages, Complexity and Edge cases. Ask who will actually use the application, what kinds of questions they ask, which languages they speak, and whether the test covers both simple and multi-step requests. Edge cases are unusual, ambiguous or difficult situations that may expose failures. The middle panel divides examples into three dataset slices. Green is Easy or Common, the typical everyday requests. Yellow is Challenging or Rare, such as a complex multi-step task. Red is Safety-Sensitive, where a mistaken answer could mislead or cause harm. Each slice shows an example prompt and a reference answer when that reference is appropriate for the metric. Now follow the right-hand validation panel. Bias asks whether results are unfair across user groups or topics. Coverage asks whether important users, languages, tasks and edge cases are represented. Leakage means the model has already seen your test items in training, which can make test performance misleading. Versioning records which dataset revision produced each score, so comparisons can be repeated. At the bottom, three puzzle pieces remind us that good results on common prompts do not guarantee success on rare or safety-sensitive ones. A sound benchmark resembles actual use and reports performance separately across these slices. A high aggregate score is not enough if one critical group performs poorly.

scenes.title: Human evaluation of foundation models
scenes.narration: Some qualities of a generated response are hard to capture with one automatic number. This slide explains a human comparison process in five stages. Start on the far left with the prompt: 'Explain in one sentence what a foundation model is.' The second panel shows candidate models A and B producing two different answers. The third panel is a blinded reviewer at a laptop. Blinded means the reviewer does not know which candidate produced each answer, reducing preference for a familiar brand or model name. In stage four, the reviewer scores each response against the rubric. Read the four rubric dimensions: helpfulness, factual grounding, instruction following and safety. Helpfulness means the response is relevant and useful. Grounding means its claims have appropriate support. Instruction following checks explicit requirements, including the request for one sentence. Safety asks whether the response avoids harmful or inappropriate content. The worked example at the bottom shows why these dimensions differ. Response A gives a compact one-sentence definition and satisfies the instruction. Response B is longer and does not meet that one-sentence requirement. In stage five, we combine reviewer ratings and inspect disagreements rather than hiding them. The example table shows Model A versus Model B: helpfulness 4.4 against 3.8, factual grounding 4.2 against 3.9, instruction following 4.8 against 2.1, and safety 4.6 against 4.3. These are illustrative averages, not guarantees about real products. The rightmost note makes another important distinction: human evaluation measures responses, whereas reinforcement learning from human feedback uses human preferences as training information. Evaluation alone does not retrain the model.

scenes.title: ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore and perplexity
scenes.narration: This slide compares four measures of language-model output quality, and each measures a different thing. Begin in the blue ROUGE panel. ROUGE is often used for summarization. It compares overlap between a generated summary and a reference summary. ROUGE-N counts matching sequences of one or more words, called n-grams, while ROUGE-L uses the longest sequence of words occurring in the same order. The little cat sentence examples illustrate overlap. Move to the purple BLEU panel. BLEU emphasizes how many generated word sequences also appear in the reference, and its brevity penalty discourages a model from winning by returning an extremely short translation. BLEU is commonly associated with machine translation. Now look at the gold BERTScore panel. The two sentences are 'The cat rests on the mat' and 'A cat is resting on a mat.' The words do not match exactly, but their meaning is similar. BERTScore uses contextual token embeddings, numerical representations informed by surrounding text, to estimate that semantic similarity. Finally, the green strip across the bottom introduces perplexity. The sequence 'The cat rests on the ...' illustrates the model predicting the next token. Lower perplexity generally means less uncertainty when predicting the same held-out corpus under a comparable setup. But perplexity is not a measurement of factual truth or safety. The decision point is simple: ROUGE emphasizes summary overlap; BLEU emphasizes translation-style sequence precision; BERTScore emphasizes semantic similarity; perplexity measures predictive uncertainty. None alone proves a response is safe, accurate or useful to the business. Choose metrics according to the task and inspect real examples alongside scores.

scenes.title: Automated evaluation in an application workflow
scenes.narration: Let's apply those evaluation ideas to the product-description workflow shown here. Follow the five panels from left to right. First we start with structured product facts about Wireless Headphones. The facts list noise cancelling, a 30-hour battery, Bluetooth 5.3, an over-ear design, USB-C charging and a Midnight Black color. These are the source details the model should stay faithful to. In panel two, a selected Amazon Bedrock text model generates a customer-facing description. Panel three shows three automated checks. Required attributes asks whether important features, such as battery life, are mentioned. Unsupported claims flags features or promises that the source facts do not justify. Reference similarity, where suitable, compares the text with trusted example descriptions using a metric such as ROUGE, BLEU or BERTScore. A high similarity score alone cannot prove correctness. In panel four, the reviewer checks a sample for accuracy, clarity, brand style and policy issues. Panel five only approves deployment when the required quality gate has passed. Now look at the two bottom sections. Offline evaluation happens before deployment, using reference examples and automated metrics. Online feedback happens after deployment, when customers interact with the description. It includes ratings, reviews, click-through, conversions, returns and broader business outcomes. The chart icon indicates monitoring results over time. This separation is important: similarity to a reference is not the same as generating sales or helping customers. In this example, a claim of forty hours of battery life would be unsupported because the supplied product data says thirty. Both automated validation and human review can help catch that error before customers see it.

scenes.title: Measure business value, not just model scores
scenes.narration: The final slide in this lesson asks a practical question: does a technically good model actually help the organization? Across the top, you can see a customer support assistant, then three outcomes to measure: quality, user feedback and business results. Start at box one below. Offline model quality measures relevance, factuality and performance across different kinds of user requests before release. These checks are important, but they are only the starting point. Box two introduces online outcomes after launch. The visible examples include user satisfaction, task completion, average revenue per user and cross-domain performance. Which of these matter depends on what the support assistant is supposed to achieve. In box three, the example focuses on operational support metrics. Helpful resolution asks whether the customer's issue was actually solved. Escalation rate measures how often the request still has to go to a human agent. Cost per resolved request considers total support cost divided by successful resolutions. Response time measures how quickly a user gets an answer. A model could be excellent at sounding polite yet fail to resolve tickets; that would produce poor business value. Box four compares a control group using the existing support experience with a treatment group using the new generative AI assistant. This is an A/B experiment. By comparing satisfaction, completion, escalation and response time across comparable groups, the team can better separate the assistant's impact from unrelated changes. A staged rollout is another way to reduce risk while measuring actual outcomes. The takeaway is to combine offline quality, feedback and real-world results. Do not choose a model merely because it wins a text metric when it does not improve the service people rely on.
